articles.title: ‘Ability to strike back’: Denmark commits to long-range missile orders
articles.snippet: Copenhagen said it would purchase Joint Strike Missiles for its F-35s and a new ground-launched munition from an American firm.
articles.full_text:
BELFAST — Denmark will acquire two types of long-range precision missiles in an effort to “strengthen national and collective deterrence,” the Nordic nation announced today.
The purchases of F-35 Joint Strike Missiles, produced by Norway’s Kongsberg, and ground-launched Anthem cruise missiles, manufactured by US firm Covenant, “are a significant step towards making Denmark better able to defend itself,” said Minister of Defence Jeppe Bruus in a statement.
He also noted that the new acquisitions send a “strong signal that we have the ability to strike back” against an adversary.
Copenhagen did not disclose the cost or quantities involved in either procurement. In a related company statement today, Kongsberg said that “negotiations with the customer” will determine the “scope and value” of the Joint Strike Missile package.
The F-35A can store the air-to-surface weapon internally to protect the fifth-generation fighter jet’s stealth profile. Denmark is on track to operate a fleet of 43 F-35’s, after pledging to acquire an additional 16 units last year.
The Anthem, meanwhile, is brand new and was only unveiled by Covenant last month. At the time, Michael Kaufman, Covenant’s co-founder and CEO, described the munition in a blog post as a “heavy-payload deep precision strike weapon system meant to fill the biggest gap in the arsenal of the West.” He went on to claim Anthem “delivers multiples of the range and payload of anything in its price class.”
Kaufman said the firm had flown the weapon more than 200 times since first flight in August 2025.
Because the long-range weapons can strike inside Russian territory, Bruus was asked during a press conference whether that could make Denmark more of a target for Moscow. As there is “an increased threat … we must be able to respond,” the minister responded, according to local outlet DR News.
It reported today that the Russian embassy said Denmark’s political direction was “aimed at a possible conflict with Russia.”
Denmark’s latest weapon acquisitions come on the heels of the country’s intelligence service warning that Russia is expected to carry out hybrid attacks at a greater frequency against NATO member states, in the near term, and there is a growing risk of a limited military attack.

articles.title: The Pentagon has gone too far in using the Other Transaction Authority. Congress should act.
articles.snippet: Created in 1958 for NASA, the obscure fiscal tool has since become the predominant approach to military contracting – at great risk to taxpayers, one researcher warns.
articles.full_text:
In the past decade, the Pentagon has increasingly relied on the Other Transaction Authority (OTA) to advance major weapon programs while skirting competition requirements and cost transparency standards. If lawmakers don’t narrow the authority, they risk sleepwalking the American people into a generation of Pentagon boondoggles.
Congress created the OTA in 1958 to provide the newly-established NASA with a flexible tool to pursue “research, development and exploration” in its race to space after the Soviets’ successful Sputnik launch. In the decades since then, lawmakers have dramatically expanded the OTA’s usage and scope, enabling elements of the Pentagon to rely on it not only for research and development, but also for weapons prototyping and production. As a result, Other Transactions have become the predominant approach to military contracting, at great risk to taxpayers.
Under the OTA, contractors are exempt from standard procurement rules specified in the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR), including competition standards, cost and pricing data requirements and accounting principles designed to protect the government from unreasonable expenses on military contracts. Put simply, the authority grants contractors the freedom to set prices on military contracts practically unilaterally, simultaneously foreclosing the possibility of government recourse should contractors price gouge the military.
Policymakers should narrow OT use for research and development purposes only, given both an increased risk of waste as well as their uncertain impact on delivery speed. The consequences of expanded OT usage simply outweigh any potential benefits.
The primary argument for increased OT use is that they deliver capabilities to the military faster than traditional FAR-based procurement contracts. However, there is little if any evidence to substantiate this claim, as the Pentagon fails to track how quickly production OTs deliver capabilities to service members relative to traditional contracts subject to competition requirements and cost transparency standards. The department releases information about how many prototyping OTs result in the production of new capabilities, either through production OTs or traditional FAR-based contracts; but according to the Government Accountability Office (GAO), past findings have been “unreliable and inaccurate.”
Another justification for OTs is that they attract new or non-traditional companies to the defense sector, increasing competition in a consolidated industry. The problem with this argument is that the Pentagon doesn’t even know what contractors are doing the work for OTs awarded through consortia. These are groups of vendors focused on specific technology domains, like naval energetic systems or aviation and missile technology. They are led by managers who receive awards from the government and then distribute work among vendors. From 2021 to 2024, the government made half of its OT obligations through consortia, yet a 2025 GAO report claims that the Pentagon cannot fully account for which vendors are carrying out OT awards.
Significant non-traditional participation in OTs is one of the four requirements that the Pentagon must fulfill to grant a prototyping project to a contractor through the OTA. In FY24, the department claimed that 93 percent of OT obligations were agreements awarded to companies in which non-traditional contractors “significantly participate.” However, the GAO maintains that the Pentagon’s ability to analyze engagement by non-traditional defense contractors (NDCs) remains limited. It lacks department-wide “aggregated data on whether OTA awardees are NDCs, the obligations they have received and their contributions to OTA projects,” casting doubt on that 93 percent claim.
To make matters worse, the legal definition of “non-traditional” is not based on the size of a company or the value of their Pentagon contracts, but on whether a company has received a Pentagon contract subject to certain accounting principles in the last year. I wrote about the importance of these principles, the Cost Accounting Standards, in Breaking Defense last year. Companies use them to determine the costs that should be charged to government contracts. Without them, contractors can assign costs to government contracts, even if they have nothing to do with government work. Despite this, Congress ultimately exempted non-traditional contractors from the Cost Accounting Standards in the FY26 NDAA. In so doing, lawmakers expanded the number of contractors considered non-traditional without broadening its legal definition – an effort that failed in the same bill.
OTs In Context
Democratic and Republican administrations alike have relied on the OTA to kickstart the prototyping and production of major weapons programs. The Biden administration relied on it to kickstart its “Replicator” program, which the Trump administration renamed the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group (DAWG). This White House has likewise relied on the OTA to advance key components of programs like the president’s theoretical missile defense shield, Golden Dome, announcing the award earlier this year of up to $3.2 billion in OTA agreements to advance the Space-Based Interceptor program and $6.5 billion in OTs to develop the Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator program and the Space Data Network.
However, the OTA obfuscates contractors’ costs, a particularly alarming lack of transparency in the case of major programs like Golden Dome or the DAWG. In FY27, the Trump administration requested nearly $55 billion for the latter program, up from $225 million in FY26. By pursuing DAWG through the OTA, the Pentagon essentially forfeits insight into the costs and profitability of components and systems integral to the program. The department effectively legalizes whatever overcharging may occur on OT agreements, making it practically invisible to the public and impeding future efforts not only to control program cost growth, but to seek reimbursement should military contractors overcharge on components.
A quick review of recent OTs suggests that typical prime contractors are significant beneficiaries of the OTA. Twelve companies received OTs to prototype Golden Dome’s Space-Based Interceptors, a third of which are prime contractors: General Dynamics Mission Systems (a business unit of General Dynamics), Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman and Raytheon (a business unit of RTX). Other recipients include Anduril, Booz Allen Hamilton and SpaceX. In addition to Space-Based Interceptors, SpaceX has also received a combined total of $6.5 billion in OTs to develop the Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator program and the Space Data Network, upon which a hypothetical Golden Dome system would depend.
OTs Gone Wild
OTs were once the exception in government contracting, but from 2016 to 2024, Pentagon obligations for prototyping and production agreements through the OTA increased tenfold, reaching over $18 billion in 2024. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has taken it a step further, releasing in 2025 two memorandums establishing OTs as a default contracting approach and directing their maximal usage. Since he released the first of these memos, Space Systems Command has increased the number of OTs by at least 470 percent, escalating an already established shift toward OTs and away from traditional FAR-based contracts.
Ultimately, prototyping and production OTs greatly increase the risk of overcharging by military contractors while doing little to ameliorate acquisition ills like schedule delays and cost overruns. However, there are options to curb the situation.
Lawmakers should help mitigate this risk by limiting OTA usage to research and development only. If they don’t, they will likely end up rubberstamping billions of dollars of Pentagon waste. Lawmakers may also rein in the OTA by repealing the non-traditional exemption from the Cost Accounting Standards, narrowing the number of contractors deemed non-traditional. Finally, the Pentagon should track how fast OTs deliver capabilities to the military relative to traditional, FAR-based contracts.
It’s irresponsible to assume, without evidence, that OTs deliver capabilities at speed. It is incumbent upon lawmakers to require the Pentagon to fill this data gap and narrow the OTA, on behalf of constituents and taxpayers.
Julia Gledhill is a Research Analyst at the Stimson Center, a foreign policy think-tank in Washington, DC. She focuses her research and writing on Pentagon spending, military contracting and weapons acquisition. She has appeared on various outlets including Al Jazeera, CNBC, NPR and Bloomberg. Julia is a regular contributor for Forbes.com, and her writing is featured in publications including The Nation, The National Interest, The Baffler and Responsible Statecraft.

articles.title: MDA awards $75M to Long Wall for low-cost, midcourse interceptor testing
articles.snippet: Long Wall is matching the Missile Defense Agency’s funding with its own capital to continue development of the Cyclops, according to the company.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Missile Defense Agency (MDA) has awarded California-based startup Long Wall $75 million to complete testing of its self-funded Cyclops low-cost interceptor designed to strike enemy missiles midway through their flight, the company announced today.
“I think it’s a first of its kind award in long-range missile defense, and a substantive commitment,” Long Wall Founder Dan Piedmont told Breaking Defense.
Long Wall officially was established in February 2025 as a rebranding of the former launch firm ABL Space Systems, with a narrow focus on missile defense.
The company unveiled the liquid-fueled Cyclops in December 2025, touting it as the first exo-atmospheric interceptor designed to be mass produced. Long Wall’s website explains that the interceptor can fit in a shipping container, and thus be launched either from the ground or from a sea-based platform. In addition, the company stresses it is largely using commercial off-the-shelf components and technology, including 3D printing, in Cyclops production.
According to the press release, the company over the past two years has invested its own capital in developing the interceptor and will continue to do so as part of the MDA contract.
“Throughout the period of performance, Long Wall will invest an additional $75 million at private expense to continue Cyclops design and development,” the release said.
The company referred a question about the duration of the contract to MDA, which did not respond by press time to a query from Breaking Defense.
While the Cyclops is a midcourse interceptor like the currently deployed Ground-Based Interceptor built by Northrop Grumman, MDA also is exploring low-cost options for destroying enemy missiles after they have reentered the atmosphere and are closer to their targets. The agency in August awarded X-Bow Systems a contract work almost $11 million to flight test its solid fuel low-cost interceptor as a potential alternative to the Army’s arsenal of Patriot missiles.

articles.title: UK proposes 14-year prison terms for undersea cable sabotage
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: In an era of hybrid threats, the British government wants to update the Submarine Telegraph Act 1885, which carries a maximum fine of £1,000 and five years’ imprisonment in cases of deliberate damage.
articles.full_text:
UK proposes 14-year prison terms for undersea cable sabotage
The British government proposed on Thursday introducing prison sentences of up to 14 years and unlimited fines for damaging undersea cables and pipelines.
It comes amid growing concerns over the vulnerability of subsea cables to so-called “hybrid warfare” by hostile states, including physical and cyberattacks targeting the cables themselves or the installations and digital systems on land.
According to the consultation’s white paper, the new criminal offenses would cover telecommunications cables, electricity interconnectors and pipelines carrying 99% of the U.K.’s international data traffic and supplying 74% of its gas.
The proposals would replace the Submarine Telegraph Act 1885, a Victorian-era law that carries a maximum fine of £1,000 — a fraction of the repair costs — and five years’ imprisonment in cases of deliberate damage.
Repairs to the Estlink 2 electricity cable between Finland and Estonia — damaged by the anchor of the Eagle S oil tanker on Christmas Day 2024 — were estimated by grid operator Elering at €50 million to €60 million ($56 million to $67 million). Attempts to prosecute senior officers of that ship are ongoing.
Under the new proposed law, alongside the 14 years for those found guilty of deliberate damage, perpetrators of reckless damage would face up to 10 years in prison and those of gross negligence up to two years.
The government said it plans to introduce statutory security and resilience requirements for subsea telecommunications operators, with powers to direct cable and repair providers on national security grounds. Separate rules would govern fiber-optic sensing technology, which can detect activity at sea but could expose sensitive information.
Telecoms minister Ian Murray and energy minister Michael Shanks said in a joint foreword that the risks to critical subsea infrastructure was involving, citing a warning earlier this year that a Royal Navy attack submarine had surfaced near a Russian spy ship mapping this infrastructure in British waters.
Matt Western, the chair of Parliament’s Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy, welcomed the proposals, stating “the legislation covering attacks on undersea cables was written in a different age and it is right that a White Paper has been brought forward to bring it up to date.”
Questions over jurisdiction in incidents of cable damage have complicated prosecutions elsewhere, alongside questions over whether they were truly reckless accidents or intentional attempts by Russia to undermine Europe.
Finnish investigators initially suspected deliberate damage, but officials from several North Sea and Baltic countries later told Recorded Future News they increasingly believed that incident and other Baltic Sea cable breaks were accidental, citing investigations, intelligence and shipping data.
The British government says the country’s cable network remains highly resilient and that most faults result from anchors, fishing nets, environmental hazards or technical failures while also warning of growing suspicious activity.
In April, the Ministry of Defence said British and allied forces had tracked a Russian attack submarine and vessels linked to Russia’s Main Directorate of Deep Sea Research, or GUGI, near cables and pipelines north of Britain, allegedly mapping such infrastructure for potential wartime sabotage.
The 12-week public consultation closes January 14, 2027.
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: Quest Diagnostics warns of potential data theft after attack on lab service system
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Nationwide lab test company Quest Diagnostics said one of its key systems may have experienced a breach of patient data.
articles.full_text:
Quest Diagnostics warns of potential data theft after attack on lab service system
A key system used by Quest Diagnostics to manage medical test results was taken offline on Thursday after the company discovered unauthorized access.
The company published a statement and an FAQ about the cyberattack, warning customers that they “believe some patient data” within the system was accessed. The platform, Quanum Lab Services Manager (LSM), is used to place test orders as well as receive and look up results.
Access to the system has been paused while Quest investigates the attack. No other part of Quest has been impacted by the cyberattack but several other systems were paused as investigators probe the breach.
Quest said it is working with law enforcement to resolve the incident and is investigating what patient data was affected by the attack.
Customers can use paper requisitions in place of the system and Quest pledged to have Quantum back up and running by Friday. The company noted in the release that the incident did not involve the recent PHP vulnerabilities causing alarm among cybersecurity experts.
A Quest spokesperson declined to comment on the nature of the incident.
Quest is one of the largest clinical laboratory companies in the U.S., reporting more than $11 billion in revenue last year.
The New Jersey-based company says it serves half of the doctors and hospitals in the U.S. and one in three American adults each year.
No hacking group has taken credit for the incident as of Thursday afternoon. Quest is one of several healthcare testing firms to report cyber incidents in 2026. Baylor Genetics recently admitted that a data breach impacted more than 2.8 million of its patients and exposed lab results, medical testing information, Social Security numbers and more.
Several other electronic health records companies dealt with attacks this year.
In response to the attacks and several others over the last two years, Congress passed a bill this month expanding federal cyber requirements for healthcare organizations that handle patient data.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Toronto crime tips org freezes operations after details of data breach come to light
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Late Wednesday night the Toronto chapter of Crime Stoppers broke ranks with the national association, revealing a timeline showing what it knew and when along with an announcement that it will pause operations.
articles.full_text:
Toronto crime tips org freezes operations after details of data breach come to light
A Toronto crime prevention program that long promised witnesses a safe space to anonymously report tips froze its operations late Wednesday night, hours after a Canadian news outlet reported that more than 1.5 million tips from Crime Stoppers chapters across the country were exposed in a data breach.
Crime Stoppers urges people not to provide their names when submitting information, but reporters at Canada’s CBC broadcaster were able to reach more than a dozen tipsters by reviewing the hacked data made available to them in March by Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets).
About half of the 1.5 million leaked tips CBC studied — some dating back 25 years — contained personal information, the outlet reported.
While Canadian Crime Stoppers Association and individual chapters, including Toronto’s, had confirmed the breach in the days after the hack, they offered no detail about what was exposed, blaming the lack of information on vendor Navigate360 and its subsidiary, P3 Global Intel.
But late Wednesday night the Toronto chapter broke ranks with the national association, revealing a timeline showing what it knew and when along with an announcement that it will pause operations.
“Since 1984, people in Toronto have come to Toronto Crime Stoppers because we promised they could stay anonymous,” Sean Sportun, chair of Toronto Crime Stoppers, said in a statement. “This week’s reporting shows that for some of them, that promise was broken. We are deeply sorry.”
The Toronto organization said it has directed Navigate360 to immediately stop taking tips and no longer process any new information. It also has told Canada’s National Anonymous Call Centre to stop receiving and processing tips meant for Toronto Crime Stoppers, according to the statement.
“Until we have a safer way to protect you, please do not send us tips by phone, online, or through the app,” the statement said.
The organization is looking for a way to take tips on a truly anonymous basis, it said.
“For more than 40 years, people in Toronto have relied on Crime Stoppers to share what they know without giving their name: a witness afraid of retaliation, a neighbour who can’t be seen talking to police, someone reporting a person close to them,” the statement said.
“Their courage has helped solve crimes, prevent tragedies, and save lives. Pausing our program means that option isn’t available now, and we did not make this decision lightly. We are pausing because those people deserve a system we can fully stand behind.”
Canadian Crime Stoppers Association and Navigate360 did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Navigate360 told Toronto Crime Stoppers that the stolen data contained 176,859 Toronto tips, which were reported between January 2022 and November 2025, the Toronto chapter’s statement said. The vendor also told Toronto Crime Stoppers that it had found 14,973 names in those tips, but could not say if the names belonged to tipsters, suspects or both.
Toronto Crime Stoppers has made “numerous requests” through their lawyers for the text of the stolen tips, but Navigate360 has not responded, the statement said.
“Since March, Navigate360 has told us repeatedly that P3 is secure,” the statement said. “In April, it told us Toronto’s data had not been taken. When it told us in June that Toronto’s data was affected, it didn’t say what was exposed.”
A hacktivist collective known as Internet Yiff Machine took responsibility for the March breach, saying its goal was to prove that Navigate360 and P3 Global Intel lied about their capabilities.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: Indian tech company eMudhra announces withdrawal from certificate business after security incident
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The issue was publicized by cybersecurity researcher Scott Helme, who published a blog saying that instead of a random 384-bit number, one of the company's private keys was just the number four.
articles.full_text:
Indian tech company eMudhra announces withdrawal from certificate business after security incident
One of the only Indian root certificate authorities trusted by major web browsers said it is withdrawing from the global certificate business after facing significant backlash over a security incident this week.
The company, eMudhra, said it was voluntarily withdrawing from the global SSL/TLS certificate business after the private keys of eight of its intermediate certificates were found to be weak, prompting browsers like Firefox, Apple and Chrome to block the certificates.
According to Google, Mozilla and several other companies, the keys could allow attackers to issue fraudulent HTTPS certificates for websites they do not control. An attacker who could intercept a user’s connection could use those certificates to impersonate websites and potentially read or modify traffic.
Cloudflare explained that the certificates were widely trusted by their own system as well as browsers and operating systems. Because of the weak keys, any attacker could create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic.
The issue was publicized by cybersecurity researcher Scott Helme, who published a blog saying that instead of a random 384-bit number, one of the private keys was just the number four. Others were simply 56 and 115.
eMudhra said this week that the certificates were created during a ceremony in April 2025 and the ”problem was a flaw in one step of the ceremony procedure.” The issue went undetected for 18 months and survived two independent audits before a researcher reverse engineered the weak keys, the company said.
eMudhra’s chairman, V. Srinivasan, said on Thursday that the company revoked the affected certificates within 14 hours of their discovery and claimed there were no compromises or data breaches as a result of the issue.
India’s Ministry of Electronics and IT said it is investigating the incident but defended the company, arguing that “some social media accounts are indulging in fear mongering about the impact of this incident.”
CERT-IN warned in its own alert that an attacker able to exploit the compromised private keys could "potentially impersonate legitimate websites or intercept or modify data exchanged between users and servers, potentially facilitating credential theft, sensitive data exposure and financial fraud."
They added that the ability to issue fraudulent certificates would also enable malicious software to appear to be digitally signed by a trusted publisher.
Withdrawing
In the announcement of its withdrawal from the certificate business, Srinivasan said it only accounted for 1% of the company’s revenue but became increasingly costly due to compliance requirements and “complexity.”
Srinivasan blamed “social media amplification” for the increased scrutiny around the company. eMudhra said it will work with browser programs and customers to transition them to other options.
“Revocation and certificate status services will keep running until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced. eMudhra will complete its remaining commitments to the browser root programs, including a full root-cause report,” the company said.
Google noted that eMudhra has committed to working with impacted subscribers to migrate customers off of the impacted root but said it is “closely investigating the ongoing inclusion of eMudhra's remaining CA certificates in the Chrome Root Store.”
Brian Fox, co-founder of cybersecurity firm Sonatype, told Recorded Future News that the issue goes far beyond browsers because certificate trust stores are embedded in dozens of products.
Each may require its own update, rebuild or release, and most organizations don’t have an inventory of where they live, he said.
“That makes this a software supply chain problem, not just a certificate revocation event. The fixes started shipping within days, but finding and adopting them is now the challenge,” he said.
“The long tail will be older releases, forgotten containers, embedded devices, and vendor tools that carry their own certificate bundles. Although now revoked, the original eMudhra-issued intermediates were not due to expire until April 2040, and outdated clients that do not process revocation information may continue trusting the affected chains until they are updated.”
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Microsoft blames ConnectWise attacks on Chinese state hacker using ARTEX AI agents
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A Chinese government-aligned hacking group used automated tools to carry out the recent supply chain attack on IT management software company ConnectWise and is using the same techniques to try to compromise organizations around the globe, Microsoft said.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft blames ConnectWise attacks on Chinese state hacker using ARTEX AI agents
A Chinese government-aligned hacking group used automated tools to carry out the recent supply chain attack on IT management software company ConnectWise and is using the same techniques to try to compromise hundreds of other organizations around the globe, Microsoft said Wednesday.
Microsoft has been investigating a string of attacks conducted by a threat actor they call Storm-0940, which has used an AI penetration testing framework called ARTEX to breach organizations’ cloud infrastructure.
Since September, the group has been able to breach a wide variety of organizations across government, aerospace, defense, finance, manufacturing, technology and energy industries.
After gaining access to the companies, the hackers conducted reconnaissance, acquired credentials and tried to expand their privileges for expanded data collection.
Microsoft said the campaign stands out because of how AI has accelerated the hackers’ ability to quickly breach targets. In multiple instances it took the threat actors less than three hours from the initial targeting to gain privileged access.
“While the majority of the targeting wasn’t successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time,” Microsoft said.
Storm-0940 has been active since 2021, according to Microsoft, and typically conducts attacks for data theft purposes. It targets internet-facing applications and uses compromised accounts to expand access.
ARTEX is a penetration testing tool that allows users to deploy any AI model to automate offensive security actions. The platform coordinates a team of agents that can “run an autonomous penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction,” Microsoft explained.
It was released on GitHub earlier this year as an open-source tool by an account known as "Autumn-27.”
The tool was recently implicated in multiple attacks on South Korean and Japanese financial institutions.
Researchers at Zscaler released a report on Wednesday saying the ARTEX-backed attacks went far beyond South Korea and targeted dozens of industries across multiple countries.
The developer of the framework — identified as Chinese cybersecurity engineer Li Puhua — released a statement on GitHub on October 8 saying the tool was abused by malicious actors.
“ARTEX was originally designed for learning and research purposes, aiming to help enterprises and organizations conduct security risk testing within their authorized assets and improve their security capabilities,” the developer wrote in a machine translated message, denying any responsibility for crimes committed with it.
“Given the misuse of the tool, the ARTEX project will no longer be updated and will be converted to closed source. No further versions or maintenance support will be released to the public.”
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning denied any knowledge of the incidents during a recent press briefing, according to Reuters.
2,900 sign-in attempts per minute
Over the weekend, ConnectWise was forced to shut down several of its services after Microsoft and other cybersecurity companies warned of a supply-chain attack impacting Cloud Backup.
The service is designed to help protect data in Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace. Attackers used stolen Cloud Backup credentials to gain wide access to any systems where the app is installed.
According to Microsoft, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate the “speed of compromised application abuse to authenticate to Microsoft 365 customer environments through applications that had already been granted access.”
“This activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and allows them to scale their operations exponentially,” Microsoft said.
“Agents are not constrained by factors affecting humans — they can work around the clock, on weekends, and on holidays and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously enabling significantly reduced time from selecting a target to achieving objectives, increasing the speed and impact of complex attacks like supply chain compromises.”
Microsoft said the ConnectWise incident involved 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute — a pace that leaves no time for human defenders to detect and respond. There were more than 111,000 failed log-on attempts on October 11 alone.
“The campaign blended broad, low-rate account spraying with sustained, high-volume authentication attempts against selected identities; 48 accounts received more than 1,000 failures, and lockout responses represented nearly 98% of all activity,” Microsoft said.
Microsoft said it was able to tie the campaign to Storm-0940 based on publicly reported IP addresses from ConnectWise that matched those seen in their own investigations.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.snippet: Expect to see quite a few websites serving "404" or "Page Not Found" errors today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
articles.full_text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.
Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.
OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.
The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.
“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”
The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.
This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.
Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

articles.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
articles.snippet: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
articles.full_text:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.
In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.
Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.
According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.
Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).
On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.
A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.
That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.
SHINYWIRE
KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.
The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.
The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.
Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).
In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.
The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”
Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.
GHOSTBYTE
According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.
A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.
“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”
It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.
Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).
In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.
“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”
The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.
CONFLICTING INTERESTS
It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.
Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.
In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).
But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.
A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.
The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.
The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.
“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”
In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.
“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.
Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.
That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.
“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”
Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.
“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

articles.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
articles.snippet: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.
As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.
The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.
“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”
In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.
TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.
Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.
“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”
As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.
Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.
Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.
Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.
That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.
“Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.”

articles.title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
articles.snippet: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today's epic patch batch dwarfs September's record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.
Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.
Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).
At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.
While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.
Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.
“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.
Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.
Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.
“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.
Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.
One has to wonder how big the backlog of flaws is at this point. Maybe this month’s increase in the number of fixes just reflects an increasing number of people working on these fixes, and that they already have enough flaws to keep them all busy for a long time. Oh to be a fly on the wall.
